sentences.text: Aiko and her family lived on Stewart Island, which is the third island of New Zealand, far to the south of the other two.
It has almost no people on it — about four hundred, all told, and most of them in one small village called Oban.
Aiko's family did not live in Oban.
They lived on the west coast, in a small wooden cabin set back from a rocky beach, three hours' walk on the coast path from the nearest neighbor.
Her father was a marine biologist and her mother made pottery, and they had chosen to live on Stewart Island because they liked the quiet.
Aiko was ten.
Her brother Kai was fifteen.
They were very different from each other.
Aiko was serious and quiet and read a lot of books.
Kai was — Aiko had thought this for years — a little bit useless.
He was a teenager.
He spent a lot of time in his room.
He said mostly one-word answers when Aiko asked him things.
He did not really help their parents around the cabin, and when he did help, he did it badly, and their mother would sigh and finish it herself.
Aiko had a small ongoing feeling about Kai — a kind of low background disappointment — that she was not really aware of but that colored every time she looked at him.
She loved him because he was her brother, but she did not think he was very good at anything.
Their father had an appointment on the mainland with a specialist.
He had been having some kind of chest problem — nobody had told Aiko exactly what it was, but her parents had been quieter than usual for the last two months, and she had noticed.
He had to go to the mainland, and their mother wanted to go with him.
It was going to be one night.
They would leave Friday morning and come back on the ferry Saturday afternoon.
Aiko and Kai would stay in the cabin.
Kai was old enough.
He had watched Aiko many times before, though usually just for an afternoon, not overnight.
"It is one night," their father said, standing on the dock, before he got in the water taxi that would take him to Oban.
"You know how to do everything.
Kai, you are in charge.
Feed the fire.
Cook the food I left in the fridge.
If anything happens, you have the radio.
If it is really bad you can call the neighbors — Mr.
and Mrs.
Kimura — and they can walk over.
Yes?" "Yes, Dad," said Kai.
He said it the way he said everything.
Short.
Not looking at his father.
Aiko rolled her eyes internally.
Their father did not seem to notice.
He kissed them both.
He got in the boat.
He and their mother waved as they pulled away.
The morning was quiet.
Aiko read.
Kai went out to help fix a section of the fence that had come loose.
He did it badly — Aiko watched from the window — but he did it.
He came back inside for lunch and made them both cheese sandwiches.
He burned the toast a little.
Aiko did not say anything.
They ate.
Kai went back to his room.
Aiko read some more.
In the afternoon Aiko went out for a walk on the beach.
That was when she noticed the weather.
The sky in the west, out over the sea, was going a strange color.
Not the normal grey.
A darker grey, almost brown.
And low.
It was moving fast.
She stood on the rocks for a while and watched.
She did not know a lot about weather but she knew a bad sky when she saw one.
She went back inside.
She said, "Kai.
Come and look at this." Kai came out of his room without hurrying.
She showed him.
He looked.
His face did not change much.
Kai went to the marine radio.
He turned it on.
He tuned to the weather channel.
They listened.
The forecaster said there was a low pressure system approaching from the Southern Ocean.
It was expected to hit the west coast of Stewart Island by evening.
Winds of 100 kilometers per hour.
Heavy rain.
Sea would be rough.
Small vessels were advised to seek shelter.
"That is more than they said this morning," Kai said.
He said it flatly.
"This morning they said we would get some rain.
Now they are saying a storm.
It has picked up more than they expected."
He was quiet for a moment.
Then he switched to the coast guard channel.
He called out.
"This is Ronaldson cabin, west coast, checking weather status." A voice came back after a moment.
A calm woman.
She said, "Ronaldson cabin, hello.
Yes, we have upgraded the alert.
This storm is moving faster than expected.
All vessels in the western sector are to remain in port.
The Oban ferry has been cancelled for tomorrow.
Please secure yourselves and prepare for a full storm event.
Do you have adults present?" Kai looked at Aiko.
Then he said into the radio, "Adults are away for medical appointment on mainland.
Only my sister and I here.
I am fifteen."
There was a small pause.
Then the calm woman said, "Copy.
Fifteen.
Are you familiar with storm procedure at your cabin." Kai said, "Yes.
I have been here for storms before.
We have supplies.
We have the fire.
We have the radio.
Kimura cabin is our nearest neighbors — about two hours' walk on the coast path." "Copy," said the woman.
"Please check in with us at 6 p.m.
and 9 p.m.
Once the storm arrives, do not attempt to walk to Kimura.
Stay in your cabin.
Ride it out.
Storm should pass by dawn.
Winds may exceed 120 kilometers per hour tonight.
Any questions?" Kai looked at Aiko.
Aiko shook her head.
She was starting to be afraid, but she did not want to say so.
"No questions," said Kai.
"Ronaldson out."
He switched off the radio.
He turned to Aiko.
He said, in a completely different voice — a voice she had never really heard him use before, a voice that was calm and clear and grown-up — "Aiko.
We have three hours.
I need you to help me.
We have a lot to do.
Are you with me?" Aiko looked at him.
She said, "Yes, Kai." She was still afraid.
But something had shifted.
